overall.sentence: The closest earlier paper, the authors' own arXiv:2409.13814 (cited as [28]), already computed the quantum shift of the GWC melting temperature with the same extended Hubbard model and Lanczos methods, at n = 1/3 and 2/3, where it is a reduction; what is new here is the extension to n = 1/2 and 1/4 (and 2/5), the finding that the shift there is upward, and the t-squared perturbative account.

assessment.claim: Headline (claims 2 and 5): at n = 1/2 and 1/4 quantum fluctuations raise the GWC melting temperature, so quantum and thermal fluctuations can compete
assessment.note: Same system, model and method as the cited [28], which found a quantum reduction of Tc at n = 1/3 and 2/3; new in the fillings and the sign. Quantum effects raising a melting or ordering temperature were reported earlier in other systems (continuum Wigner crystal, 2504.04538 [46]; pyrochlores [47, 48]), all cited. No earlier paper in 9 arXiv searches reports an increase for a lattice GWC.

assessment.claim: Claim 3 and p. 2: 'To the best of our knowledge, no previous study has addressed' the classical-theory versus experiment Tc gap at other fillings; quantum effects move Tc toward experiment
assessment.note: [28] treated the gap at n = 1/3 and 2/3 (stated in the paper); the uncited 2408.14553 computed quantum and thermal melting temperatures of GWCs in TMD heterobilayers with a phonon-Lindemann method, so the question and system are shared but not the method or the filling-by-filling comparison with experiment.

positioning: The paper extends the authors' finite-temperature Lanczos study of GWC melting at n = 1/3 and 2/3 (arXiv:2409.13814, [28]) to n = 1/4, 1/2 and 2/5, and reports that quantum fluctuations raise Tc at 1/2 and 1/4, with a perturbative t-squared account and a domain-wall picture at 1/3. Other GWC melting work treats zero-temperature quantum melting (Morales-Duran et al., Zhou-Sheng-Kim), classical Monte Carlo intermediate phases (Matty-Kim) or a phonon-Lindemann estimate of melting temperatures (2408.14553, not cited); none found in 9 arXiv searches computes the sign of the hopping-induced Tc shift at these fillings. No named earlier paper contradicts a priority statement: one B item asks the authors to cite the Lindemann study next to their 'no previous study' sentence, and one C item narrows the abstract's general framing; a later experiment (2609.30788, posted after this paper) reports an entropy-stabilized GWC at 1/3 and 1/4 and is useful context.

issues.claim: Including quantum effects shifts the theoretical melting temperatures toward experiment
issues.headline: Uncited study of GWC quantum and thermal melting temperatures
issues.issue: The phonon-Lindemann study 'Stability of Wigner crystals and Mott insulators in twisted moiré structures' (arXiv:2408.14553, 2024), already computed quantum and thermal melting temperatures of GWCs in TMD heterobilayers. It is not cited, and a referee who knows it may question the 'no previous study' sentence.

evidence.quote: To the best of our knowledge, no previous study has addressed the issue of the considerable difference between the transition temperature of the (classical) theory and experiment for various other fillings, as Table I shows.
evidence.location: Main text, p. 2, right column, paragraph after Eq. (3)

issues.fix: Cite arXiv:2408.14553 here and say what differs: it estimates GWC melting temperatures from a harmonic phonon expansion and the Lindemann criterion, while this work computes the hopping-induced Tc shift filling by filling with exact many-body methods and compares it with experiment.

edit.before: To the best of our knowledge, no previous study has addressed the issue of the considerable difference between the transition temperature of the (classical) theory and experiment for various other fillings, as Table I shows.
edit.after: Melting temperatures of GWCs have been estimated from phonon expansions with the Lindemann criterion [ref: arXiv:2408.14553], but, to our knowledge, the considerable difference between the classical and experimental transition temperatures at the other fillings in Table I has not been addressed with many-body calculations.

issues.claim: Quantum and thermal fluctuations can be competitive, raising the melting temperature
issues.headline: Abstract framing implies the competition is shown here first
issues.issue: The abstract sets the result against a general belief, but the paper itself cites earlier cases where quantum effects raise a melting or ordering temperature: the continuum Wigner crystal (arXiv:2504.04538, [46]) and quantum pyrochlores ([47, 48]). These appear only in the conclusion, so a referee may read the abstract as claiming more generality than it shows.

evidence.quote: We show that this is not always the case and that the interplay between quantum and thermal fluctuations can be competitive.

issues.fix: Say the competition is shown for GWCs and cite the earlier examples ([46-48]) in the introduction where the general belief is stated.

edit.before: We show that this is not always the case and that the interplay between quantum and thermal fluctuations can be competitive.
edit.after: We show that for generalized Wigner crystals this is not always the case and that, as in some other systems, the interplay between quantum and thermal fluctuations can be competitive.
